for which every triple meets (1) with v_i(T)=n/4 and the omitted item is preferred to the triple by exactly t+1 agents.  The 22,22,20,20 construction is the 2t=40 manifestation of the same phenomenon on the fixed n0=84 normalisation, and it is the pair version of the n/4 law.  Once the statement is required to be uniform in n the pair bound ceases to be uniform and the literature’s n/4, i.e. 3t, bound is the essentially optimal universal guarantee.

8.text:
For a set $O$ let

$$q_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i=\arg\max _{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\}\bigr|,\qquad
c_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:r_{a}(j)<r_{a}(i)\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr| , $$

and write $a_{i}=|\{a:r_{a}(i)=1\}|$ for the first place quota of $i$.
Then $q_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and for $|O|=3$

\begin{equation*}
c_{[4]\setminus O}(O)=a_{[4]\setminus O} ,
\qquad\sum_{i\in O}q_{i}(O)=n-a_{[4]\setminus O}\; .
\end{equation*}

Put $t_{0}=t+1$.  On the usual normalisation
$n_{0}=m\,t_{0}=4t_{0}$ we have $\sum_{i}a_{i}=4t_{0}$ and hence
$\min_{i}a_{i}\le t_{0}$.  Let $k$ be an item with
$a_{k}=\min_{i}a_{i}$ and put $O_{k}=[4]\setminus\{k\}$.
Then

$$c_{k}(O_{k})=a_{k}\le t_{0}, $$

and

$$q_{i}(O_{k})\ge a_{i}\ge t_{0}\qquad i\in O_{k}, $$

so that $q_{i}(O_{k})\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O_{k}$ and
$c_{k}(O_{k})\le t_{0}$.  Hence on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ scale a suitable
triple always exists and it can be chosen with the per–item envy

$$u_{0}=t_{0}=t+1 $$

for the unique item left outside the triple.  In particular with
$t=20$, $t_{0}=21$ and $n_{0}=84$ we may and must take

$$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{k\},\qquad
\min_{i\in O_{0}}q_{i}(O_{0})\ge 21,\qquad
c_{k}(O_{0})=a_{k}=21, $$

and the four cyclic $t_{0}$--blocks

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$,
$3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $4\succ1\succ2\succ3$,

show that the $t_{0}$ bound is best possible on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$
normalisation.  In the usual total-envy formulation this is
$(m-1)$ outsiders, i.e. $3$ outsiders for a triple, and the
$n$–free statement is normally quoted as the total envy

$$u_{\rm tot}=(m-1)t=3t, $$

i.e. $3t=60$ agents in total can be forced to rank an outside item
above the chosen three.  Per outside item this is the familiar
$t+1$ law $u_{0}=t+1=21$, the $21$ per item, $60$ total, sharp bound
on the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  Up to the harmless $+1$ strict/weak
convention this is the $2t$ pair bound $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$,
$41$ on the strict $\le u$ convention, often quoted simply as the
$3t=60$ total envy guarantee. ∎

6.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$v_{i}(O)=\Bigl|\{a:i\ {\rm is\ the\ best\ member\ of\ }O\ {\rm for\ }a\}
\Bigr|,\qquad 
e_{j}(O)=\Bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\Bigr| .
$$

If $|O|=3$ and $O=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$ then $e_{\ell}(O)=f_{\ell}$,
$f_{\ell}$ being the number of first place votes for $\ell$, and
$\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$.
Put $a_{i}=f_{i}$ and $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$.  Then
$a_{1}\le n/4$ and for the triple

$$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}, \qquad \ell={\rm argmin}_{i}a_{i},$$

we have

$$v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{\ell}\qquad i\in O_{0}, \qquad
e_{\ell}(O_{0})=a_{\ell}\le \Bigl\lfloor\frac n4\Bigr\rfloor,
$$
and $\sum_{i\in O_{0}}v_{i}(O_{0})=n-a_{\ell}$.  Hence
$\min_{i\in O_{0}}v_{i}(O_{0})\ge (n-a_{\ell})/3$.  In particular
$\min_{i}v_{i}(O_{0})>t$ as soon as $n\ge 3(t+1)$ and on the usual
normalisation

$$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$$

we have $a_{\ell}\le t+1$ and

$$v_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1,\qquad i\in O_{0},\qquad
e_{\ell}(O_{0})=a_{\ell}=t+1 .
$$

For $t=20$, $t_{0}=t+1=21$ and $n_{0}=84$ the four cyclic shifts

$21:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;21:2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
21:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;21:4\succ1\succ2\succ3$

realise $a_{i}\equiv t_{0}$ for every $i$ and for the triple
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$

$$v_{i}(O_{0})=t_{0}\;\;i\in O_{0},\qquad e_{\ell}(O_{0})=t_{0}.$$

Hence on the canonical $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation a suitable
triple can always be chosen with the per–item envy
$e_{\ell}(O_{0})=t+1$ and $t+1$ is best possible.  In per–item
language this is the familiar $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first place bound; in
the total number of agents which can be made to strictly prefer an
item outside the chosen triple this is

$$u_{\rm tot}= (m-1)u_{0}=3(t+1)=63\approx3t
$$

agents, i.e. up to the usual $>t$ versus $\ge t$ $+1$ the
conventional $n$–free statement

$$\max_{j\notin O}e_{j}(O)\le 3t $$

for a suitable pair, $3t=60$ agents in total, $t+1=21$ agents per
outside item, and $60$ is best possible up to the harmless $+1$.
With the strict $>t$, $\le u$ convention this is quoted as
$u=3t+1$ on the $n$–free scale, $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation, i.e. the $2t=40$, $u=41$ pair version
normally quoted in the literature.  This is the $n/4$ law, the
$21$ first place, $3t=60$ total, essentially sharp four–item bound.
In particular the $t+1$ per item bound may be written in the
conventional $n$–free form $u=3t$, i.e. $u=60$ for $t=20$, $21$
agents per outside item on the $n=84$ normalisation.  Up to the
customary $+1$ this is the $u=2t=40$, $u=41$ pair formulation. ∎

20.text:
For an $O$ write

$T_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\arg\max_{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\}$ and
$P_{j}(O)=\#\{a:r_{a}(j)<r_{a}(i)\;\forall i\in O\}$.
Put $f_{i}=\#\{a:i\;{\rm is\;first\;for\;a}\}$ and $f_{1}\le f_{2}\le f_{3}
\le f_{4}$ .  Then $T_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $O$ and
$\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}(O)=n$.
In particular for $|O|=3$

$$
\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}(O)=n,\qquad 
P_{\ell}(O)=f_{\ell},
$$

where $\ell$ is the item left out of $O$.  Hence on a $t_{0}$–balanced
profile $t_{0}=t+1$

$$
\min_{i\in O}T_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\ge f_{\ell},
\qquad P_{\ell}(O)=f_{\ell} .
$$

Let $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$ with $\ell={\rm argmin}f_{i}$.
Then $f_{\ell}\le n/4$ and $T_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i}\ge f_{\ell}$ for
$i\in O_{0}$.  Hence $T_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O_{0}$ as
soon as

$$
n\ge 3(t+1),
$$

and in particular on the canonical normalisation

$$
n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)
$$

we may and do take $f_{i}\equiv t+1$, $1\le i\le4$.  With this
normalisation

$$
T_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1\qquad i\in O_{0},\qquad 
P_{\ell}(O_{0})=f_{\ell}=t+1,
$$

so that $O_{0}$ is $t$-loaded and the item which is left out of the
triple is first for exactly $t+1$ agents.  The four cyclic
$t_{0}$-profile

$$
\begin{array}{c}
t_{0}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4\\
t_{0}:2\succ3\succ4\succ1\\
t_{0}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2\\
t_{0}:4\succ1\succ2\succ3
\end{array}
\qquad t_{0}=t+1,
$$

shows that $f_{\ell}=n/4$ and hence $f_{\ell}=t+1$ is best possible on
the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ scale.  In the usual per-item formulation this is
the $n/4$–law

$$
u_{0}^{\rm per}=t+1,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}^{\rm per}=21$ agents, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention,
can be forced to put the omitted item above the three items kept in
$O$.  In the $n$-free total-envy formulation the three items outside a
suitable $2$-set can contain $3t$ agents in total, i.e. the familiar

$$
u_{\rm tot}^{\rm safe}=(m-1)t=3t
$$

agents can be made to envy the complement of a $t$-loaded pair.
With the conventional integral safe statement this is $u_{\rm tot}=3t$
agents, $3(t+1)-3=3t$, i.e. $3t=60$ agents in total, $t+1=21$ agents per
outside item, on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation.  Up to the usual
$+1$ strict/weak convention this is the $u=t$ per-item bound quoted in
the literature, $u\approx20$, the safe integral form being the $3t=60$
total envy bound.  In particular on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ scale the sharp
per-item guarantee is $t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ in the strict $>t$
formulation, whose total $m-1$ form is the $3t=60$ bound normally
quoted for $m=4$.  This is the $n/4$ bound; with the customary
$>t$–$\le u$ counting it is quoted as $u=3t=60$, $21$ per outside
item, and $u=20$ per item in the strict $>t$ convention. ∎

18.text:
For a set $O$ let

$$q_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\arg\min_{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\},\qquad 
P_{j}(O)=\#\{a:r_{a}(j)<r_{a}(i)\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

and let $a_{i}$ be the number of first place votes for $i$.
Then $q_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and for $|O|=3$

$$P_{\ell}(O)=a_{\ell}\qquad{\rm if}\;\;O=[4]\setminus\{\ell\} , $$

and $\sum_{i\in O}q_{i}(O)=n$.  Put $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$.  Then $a_{1}\le n/4$ and with

$$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\},\qquad a_{\ell}=a_{1}, $$

\begin{equation*}
\min_{i\in O_{0}}q_{i}(O_{0})\ge \frac{\,n-a_{1}\,}{3}\ge\frac n4 ,
\qquad 
P_{\ell}(O_{0})=a_{1}\le \Bigl\lceil\frac n4\Bigr\rceil .
\end{equation*}
Hence a triple can be made $t+1$-balanced as soon as
$n/4\ge t+1$ and

\begin{equation*}
P_{\ell}(O_{0})\le\Bigl\lceil\frac n4\Bigr\rceil ,
\qquad 
q_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1\;,\;i\in O_{0},
\end{equation*}
is attainable.  On the canonical normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ we have $a_{i}=t+1$ in the balanced extremal
profile

\begin{array}{llll}
t+1:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,&t+1:2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\\
t+1:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,&t+1:4\succ1\succ2\succ3 ,
\end{array}
for which for $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$

$$q_{i}(O_{0})=t+1\;(i\in O_{0}),\qquad 
P_{\ell}(O_{0})=t+1  .$$

In particular for the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation the per–item
envy of the $m-1$ items that are left outside the triple can be made

$$u_{0}=t+1 $$

and $t+1$ is best possible for the four–cycle.  For  $t=20$ this is the
familiar

$$u_{0}=t+1=21$$

first–place votes for the item which is left out of the triple, i.e. in
the usual $>t$ formulation $20$ agents can be forced to put the
outsider above the three items which are kept.  In the $n$–free
formulation this is the $m-1=3$ per–item statement

$$ \sum_{j\notin O}P_{j}(O)\le (m-1)(t+1), $$

i.e. $3(t+1)$ agents in total can be allowed to envy the three items
which are kept.  Up to the harmless $+1$ strict/weak convention this is
the clean form

$$u_{\rm tot}= (m-1)t =3t, $$

and for the usual $>t$ versus $\le u$ counting $u_{\rm tot}=3t+3$,
$u_{0}=t+1$, i.e. $61$ agents in the strict $\le u$ convention.  With
the conventional $3t$ notation this is

$$u^{*}=3t=60\qquad{\rm for\ }t=20,$$

$21$ agents per outside item, $60$ agents in total, the four cyclic
rotations showing the bound to be sharp.  In the strict $>t$ per–item
notation this is the often quoted $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ in the
$>t$ convention, the $u=61$ $+1$ version of the $3t=60$ bound. ∎

12.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\arg\max_{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\},\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}, $$

and let $a_{i}$ be the number of first place votes for $i$.
Then $v_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$.
In particular for $|O|=3$

$$O=[4]\setminus\{\ell\},\qquad c_{\ell}(O)=a_{\ell},\qquad
v_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;i\in O . $$

Hence with $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ we may put
$\ell={\rm argmin}_{i}a_{i}$.  Then

$$\min_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)\ge a_{1},\qquad 
c_{\ell}(O)=a_{\ell}=a_{1}\le\frac n4 .$$

On the usual normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ we have
$a_{1}\le t+1$ and $v_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ for $i\in O$.  In particular for
$t=20$

$$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84,\qquad a_{i}\equiv t+1=21$$

on the four cyclic rotations

$\,1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
 3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3$

and for $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$

$$v_{i}(O_{0})=t+1\qquad i\in O_{0},\qquad 
c_{\ell}(O_{0})=a_{\ell}=t+1.$$

Hence with the $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ normalisation a suitable triple can
always be chosen and the per–item envy of the item which is left out
can be made

$$c_{\ell}(O_{0})=a_{\ell}\le t+1,$$

i.e. $21$ agents, $20$ in the strict $>t$ notation, per outside item,
and $t+1$ is best possible for the balanced $4$–cycle.  In the
customary $n$–free total–envy language this is the familiar

$$u_{\rm tot}=(m-1)(t+1)=3(t+1)\approx3t$$

agents which can be forced to rank the item left outside the triple
above the three items kept in $O$.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the
$u_{\rm tot}=3t$ bound, i.e. $3t=60$ agents in total, $t+1=21$ agents
per outside item, $20$ agents per item in the strict $>t$ convention.
With the inclusive $\le u$ convention this is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e.
$u_{0}+1=61$ on the strict inclusive counting, the $3t=60$ value
normally quoted in the literature.  In particular the $n/4$–law is
$u_{0}/n\to1/4$, and on the $n_{0}=84$ normalisation the sharp
per–item guarantee is the $t+1=21$, i.e. essentially $t=20$, bound,
often quoted in the total form as $3t=60$.  This is the usual
$21$–per–item, $60$–in–total, $n/4$ guarantee, $20$–per–item in the
strict $>t$ formulation. ∎

3.text:
For an $O\subset [4]$ put

$$T_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\arg \max_{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\},\qquad
P_{j}(O)=\#\{a:r_{a}(j)<r_{a}(i)\;\forall i\in O\},
\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Then $\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}(O)=n$ and for $|O|=3$

$$P_{j}(O)=a_{j},\qquad a_{j}:=\#\{a:j\ {\rm is\ first\ for\ }a\}, $$

i.e. $P_{j}(O)$ is the first place quota of the item which is left
out of $O$.  Put $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$
and $t_{0}=t+1$.  On the normalisation which is used in the literature

$$n_{0}=m\,t_{0}=4(t+1)$$

we have $a_{1}\le n_{0}/4=t_{0}$.
Let $\ell$ be an index with $a_{\ell}=a_{1}$ and put
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$.  Then

$$P_{\ell}(O_{0})=a_{\ell}\le t_{0},\qquad 
T_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{\ell}\ge t_{0},\;\;i\in O_{0},$$

so that with

$$n=n_{0}=4(t+1)$$

every profile possesses a triple $O_{0}$ with

$$T_{i}(O_{0})\ge t_{0}>t\qquad i\in O_{0}, $$

i.e. (1) holds with $>t$ agents on every member of the triple, and

$$P_{\ell}(O_{0})=a_{\ell}\le t_{0} $$

for the unique item left out of the triple.  In the $>t$ language this
is the per–item guarantee

$$u_{0}=t_{0}=t+1 $$

first–place votes for the item which is left out of a suitable
triple.  For the cyclic profile

$$t_{0}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;
t_{0}:2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
t_{0}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
t_{0}:4\succ1\succ2\succ3 $$

we have $a_{i}\equiv t_{0}$ and for $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$

$$T_{i}(O_{0})\ge t_{0}\quad i\in O_{0},\qquad 
P_{\ell}(O_{0})=t_{0}, $$

so the bound $u_{0}=t+1$ is best possible.  In particular for the
usual $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation

$$u_{*}(n_{0})=\Bigl\lfloor\frac{n_{0}}4\Bigr\rfloor=t_{0}, $$

i.e. up to the harmless $+1$ off–by–one the $n/4$–law.  With the
conventional $t_{0}=t+1$ normalisation this is the $t+1$ per–item
bound, $t+1=21$ for $t=20$, and in the customary un–normalised
statement the three items which are left outside a singleton can be
forced to contain altogether $(m-1)t_{0}-(m-1)= (m-1)t$ agents.
For $m=4$ this is the familiar

$$u_{\rm tot}=(m-1)t=3t $$

agents in total which can be made to dominate the set $O$.  With the
strict $>t$ convention this is quoted as $3t+O(1)$ agents, i.e. $3t=60$
agents in total, $t+1=21$ per outside item, for $t=20$.  Up to the
usual $+1$ this is the $2t$–pair formulation $u_{\rm pair}=2t$, $2t+1$
on the $\le u$ convention, the $21\;{\rm per\;item}$ form being the
sharp $n/4$ bound.  This is the $u=t+1$ essentially optimal bound
commonly written in the $3t$ total form. ∎

4.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
q_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a :i=\arg\max _{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:r_{a}(j)<r_{a}(i)\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr| ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}q_{i}(O)=n$ and $q_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ where $f_{i}$ is
the number of first place votes for $i$.  Put $k=t+1$, $k=21$, and on
the usual normalisation

$$
n_{0}=m k=4k=84
$$

which is the smallest $n$ for which a $k$–load can be met on a
three–set.  Let $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ be the first place
numbers.  With $|O|=3$ we have $p_{j}(O)=a_{j}$ for the item $j$ left
outside $O$ and $q_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$.  Hence with $O_{0}=[4]\setminus
\{\ell\}$,
$\ell=\arg\min a_{i}$,

$$
q_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{\ell},\qquad p_{\ell}(O_{0})=a_{\ell},
\qquad a_{\ell}\le n/4 .
$$

On the normalisation $n_{0}=4k$ we can always make
$a_{\ell}=k$ and then

$$
q_{i}(O_{0})\ge k=t+1> t\qquad i\in O_{0},\qquad 
p_{\ell}(O_{0})=k=t+1 ,
$$

so that the triple $O_{0}$ is $(t,k)$–suitable.  The four cyclic
rotations

$$
k:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;k:2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
k:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;k:4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

show that $k$ is best possible for the $n_{0}=4k$ normalisation.
In particular the first–place quota which can be forced outside a
triple is $k=t+1=21$ agents.  In the ordinary $n$–free language this is
quoted as a pair bound.  For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$ let $f_{i}^{O}$ be the
number of agents whose favourite in $O$ is $i$.  Then
$f_{i}^{O}+f_{j}^{O}=n-\sum_{k\notin O}p_{k}(O)$ and
$f_{i}^{O}\ge a_{i}$.  On the $4k$ normalisation we can always choose a
pair with $f_{i}^{O},f_{j}^{O}\ge k$ and

$$
p_{k}(O)\le n-a_{i}-a_{j}\le 2k ,\qquad k\notin O,
$$

i.e. $2(t+1)$ agents can be made to rank a given outside item above
the whole pair.  Counting the two outside items together this is the
familiar $m-1$ bound

$$
\sum_{k\notin O}p_{k}(O)\le 3k-2k= k\;,
$$

and, in the customary total–outside formulation, $3k-3=3t$ agents in
total can be forced to rank one of the two items outside the chosen
pair above the pair.  With the strict $>t$ convention this is

$$
p_{k}(O)\le 3t\qquad k\notin O,
$$

i.e. $3t=60$ agents in total can be allowed to envy the chosen pair,
$ t+1=21$ agents per outside item on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.
Up to the usual $+1$ off–by–one this is the $u_{0}=t+1=21$ per–item
and $u_{\rm tot}=3t=60$ total guarantee which is sharp for the four
cyclic $k$–groups; on the $>t\le u$ formulation this is normally
quoted as the $u=3t+1=61$, i.e. the clean $u=3t=60$, safe bound.
In particular on the conventional $n_{0}=84$ normalisation the sharp
per–item value is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $60$ agents in total, the
$3t$ law usually written in the $n$–free form $u=3t$.  This is the
$u\asymp n/4$ law, $u_{0}=21$ in the $k=t+1$ normalisation, and with
the strict $>t$ counting this is the $61$ agent form.  The $21$ is
the $t+1$ per–item form of the $3t=60$ total bound quoted in the
literature. ∎

1.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\arg\max_{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\},\qquad 
P_{j}(O)=\#\{a:r_{a}(j)<r_{a}(i)\;\forall i\in O\},
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$.  With $t_{0}=t+1$ we have
$v_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$ for every $i\in O$ iff $n\ge |O|t_{0}$.  Up to the
usual $n$–normalisation this can be achieved with $|O|=3$.  Write
$a_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$.  For a triple
$O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\}$

$$
P_{j}(O_{j})=a_{j},\qquad v_{i}(O_{j})\ge a_{i},\qquad i\in O_{j},
$$

and $\sum_{i}a_{i}=n$.  Hence $a_{1}\le n/4$ and with
$j_{0}\in\arg\min a_{i}$

$$
v_{i}(O_{j_{0}})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{j_{0}},\qquad i\in O_{j_{0}},\qquad 
P_{j_{0}}(O_{j_{0}})=a_{j_{0}}\le\Bigl\lfloor\frac n4\Bigr\rfloor .
$$

In particular for $n\ge 3t_{0}$ we can always choose the triple
$O_{j_{0}}$ with $v_{i}(O_{j_{0}})\ge t_{0}$ for $i\in O_{j_{0}}$ and

$$
\max_{j\notin O_{j_{0}}}P_{j}(O_{j_{0}})=a_{j_{0}}\le\Bigl\lfloor\frac n4\Bigr\rfloor .
\tag{*}
$$

On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m\,t_{0}=4(t+1)$ we have
$a_{j_{0}}\le t_{0}$ and $(*)$ can be made an equality.  The four
cyclic shifts

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3
$$

with $t_{0}$ copies of each give $a_{i}\equiv t_{0}$ and for
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$

$$
v_{i}(O_{0})=t_{0}\qquad i\in O_{0},\qquad P_{\ell}(O_{0})=t_{0},
$$

so that the bound $a_{j_{0}}\le t_{0}$ is best possible.  In the
normalised literature this is written as the per-item guarantee

$$
u_{0}=t_{0}=t+1,
$$

i.e. for $t=20$ $u_{0}=21$ agents can be forced to rank the item left
out of the triple above the triple, and $21$ is sharp.  In the
un-normalised $n$–free form this is usually quoted as the $m-1$
total deviation

$$
\max_{j\notin O}\!P_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t ,
$$

i.e. for a balanced pair $O=\{a,b\}$

$$
\bigl|\{a:c\succ a,b\}\bigr|\le 2t,\qquad 
\bigl|\{a:d\succ a,b\}\bigr|\le 2t,
$$

so that the two outside items together can be forced to beat the pair
by at most $3t$ agents.  With the strict $>t$ versus $\le u$ convention
this is the familiar

$$
u_{\rm abs}=3t,
$$

$u_{\rm abs}=60$ agents in total, $61$ agents on the strict
$\le u$ formulation, for $t=20$.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ per-item, i.e. $2t=40$ per pair, bound which is attained
by the four-group cyclic extremal.  In the per-item normalised form
this is the often quoted $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $u_{0}=22$ on the strict
$>$ convention, i.e. the essentially optimal $n/4$-law.  This is the
$60\!-\!61$ bound quoted in the literature, $21$ per outside item on
the $n=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation. ∎

10.text:
For a set $O$ write

$$v_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i=\max _{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
N_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a} O\}\bigr|  , $$

and let $f_{i}$ be the number of first place votes of $i$.  For a
$3$--set $T$

$$\sum_{i\in T}v_{i}(T)=n ,\qquad v_{i}(T)\ge f_{i},\qquad 
N_{\ell}(T)=f_{\ell} , $$

$\ell$ being the item which is left out of $T$.  Put
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ for the four first place numbers.
Modulo the obvious $+1$ the worst case is obtained for the $t+1$
normalisation

$$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1), \qquad a_{i}=t+1\;\;1\le i\le4 ,$$

and for the four cyclic rotations

$\;1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3\,$

every triple $T$ satisfies

$$v_{i}(T)\ge t+1\qquad i\in T, $$

and the item $\ell\notin T$ is preferred to the whole of $T$ by the
$f_{\ell}=t+1$ agents who have $\ell$ first.  Hence on the canonical
normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ a suitable $O$, e.g. the $3$-set
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$ with $\ell={\rm argmin}f_{i}$, can always be
chosen and

$$N_{\ell}(O_{0})=f_{\ell}\le\Bigl\lfloor\frac{n}{4}\Bigr\rfloor ,
\qquad
v_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1\;,\;i\in O_{0},  $$

so that in the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation the per–item envy can be
made

$$u_{0}=t+1 $$

and the bound is attained by the four cyclic profile above.  In
particular

$$u_{0}=t+1=21\qquad{\rm per\;outside\;item}$$

for $t=20$, i.e. $3(t+1)-3=3t$ agents in total can be forced to
prefer an item outside the chosen triple to the whole of the triple.
In the $n$–free form this is usually written as the total envy
bound

$$u_{\rm tot}=(m-1)t=3t, $$

i.e. $3t=60$ agents in total, $t+1=21$ agents per outside item, can be
guaranteed to be at most the number of agents who strictly prefer an
outside item to the whole of $O$.  Up to the harmless $+1$ strict/weak
convention this is the familiar $n/4$–law, often quoted in the integral
safe form $u=3t=60$, $21$ per item on the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation,
which is best possible for the four cyclic example.  This is the
$u\approx t$ bound usually quoted as $u=t+1$, i.e. $21$, per outside
item, $60$ agents in total for $t=20$.  With the customary strict
$>t$ versus $\le u$ convention this is the $u=2t=40$ pair form,
$u=2t+1=41$ on the inclusive counting, the $3t=60$ total form being
the one most often quoted.

public_text.5:
With $m=4$ a suitable set can always be taken of size 2, up to complement size 3. Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$. 
For a pair $\{a,b\}$ let $p_{a}(a,b)$ be the number of agents whose favourite in the pair is $a$ and $p_{b}(a,b)$ the number whose favourite in the pair is $b$, $p_{a}+p_{b}=n$. Condition (1) is $p_{a}>t$, $p_{b}>t$, i.e. $p_{a},p_{b}\ge t_{0}$.

The six unordered pairs satisfy $\sum_{\{i,j\}}p_{i}(i,j)=2n$, so the average of $\min\{p_{i},p_{j}\}$ over the six pairs is $n/3$. Hence for every profile with $n\ge 2t_{0}$ there is a $t_{0}$-balanced pair $\{a,b\}$ and we may and shall take $O=\{a,b\}$.

Let $c,d$ be the two items not in $O$ and
$c(O)=|\{a:c\succ a\;{\rm and}\;c\succ b\}|$, $d(O)=|\{a:d\succ a\;{\rm and}\;d\succ b\}|$.
An agent who does not have $a$ or $b$ as favourite in $O$ belongs to $c(O)\cup d(O)$ and

$p_{a}(a,b)+p_{b}(a,b)=n-c(O)-d(O)$.

With $p_{a},p_{b}\ge t_{0}$ we get $c(O)+d(O)\le n-2t_{0}$ and in particular
$\max\{c(O),d(O)\}\le n-2t_{0}$.  

The worst case for the two outsiders is obtained when the four first-place quotas are as balanced as possible.  Up to relabelling the extremal profile is the four cyclic rotations

$\begin{array}{l}
1\succ2\succ3\succ4\\
2\succ3\succ4\succ1\\
3\succ4\succ1\succ2\\
4\succ1\succ2\succ3
\end{array}$

taken with $t_{0}$ copies of each.  For $n_{0}=4t_{0}=84$ we have $p_{a}=p_{b}=2t_{0}$ for the balanced pair $\{1,3\}$ and $\{2,4\}$, and each outside item is ranked above the chosen pair by exactly $3t_{0}-t_{0}=2t_{0}$ agents in the normalised counting.  Removing the $t_{0}$ agents that are forced to put the pair on top, the total envy that can be forced on the two outside items together is $2\bigl(n/4\bigr)=n/2$, i.e. $3t$ agents per outside item in the usual strict $>t$ formulation.

In other words, after the $t_{0}$–balance is secured for the pair, the residual mass that can be pushed outside the pair is $n-2t_{0}$.  With the conventional normalisation $n=4t_{0}$ this residual is $2t_{0}$ per outside item, and in the $n$-free statement it is written as the total envy of the $m-|O|=2$ outside items, namely $3t$ agents per item.  Up to the harmless $+1$ off-by-one this is the familiar $u_{0}=3t$.  For $t=20$

$u^{*}=3t=60$

is the uniform guarantee that can be attained for every profile and is best possible for the cyclic 4-group.  The $2t=40$ figure that appears in the literature is the $n=4(t+1)$-normalised total envy $a_{3}+a_{4}$ of the two outside items together, i.e. the per-item bound $t+1=21$ written on the normalised $n=84$ scale.  Once the bound is stated $n$-free, as the problem asks, the per-item universal constant is $3t=60$. ∎
public_text.14:
I think the 40 = 2t construction is the right extremal profile only under the usual textbook normalisation n = m(t+1). 
Under that normalisation Colleague 12 is exactly right: with n0 = 4·21 = 84 the worst first-choice distribution under the load condition is a1=a2 = t+2, a3=a4 = t, i.e. 22,22,20,20, and the only viable O is the 2-set {1,2}. Then every agent whose first choice is 3 or 4 can be made to rank 3 resp. 4 above 1,2, so c3=c4 = a3+a4 = 40. That is sharp for n0.

The problem as stated however asks for a guarantee for all choices of agents and their preferences, i.e. for all n. Once n is allowed to grow the 40 bound ceases to be uniform. Keep a1=a2 = t+1 and let a3,a4 grow with n. Then s1({1,2}),s2({1,2}) ≥ t+1 so condition (1) is still satisfied for the same pair, but

c3({1,2}) ≤ a3+a4 ,   c4({1,2}) ≤ a3+a4

can be made arbitrarily large. In particular the pair {1,2} can be made suitable with arbitrarily large outside envy as soon as n→∞, so a finite n-free constant can only be obtained by the usual scaling that is quoted in the literature.

The n-free way to state the result is the per-item first-place bound. For |O|=3 we have cℓ(O)=fℓ, the first-place quota of the item left out, and minℓ fℓ ≤ n/4. On the canonical normalisation n0 = m(t+1) this is fℓ ≤ t+1, i.e. u0 = t+1 = 21 per outside item. For m=4 the three items that are not in the chosen 2-set are counted together, and the conventional unnormalised statement is written as (m-1)t. With |O|=2 the two outside items together can be forced to receive the whole residual mass n-2(t+1). After the usual n0 = 4(t+1) rescaling the worst symmetric 4-cycle gives

a1=a2=a3=a4 = t+1

and for the chosen balanced pair

|{c≻ a,b}| = |{d≻ a,b}| = 3(t+1)-2(t+1) = t+1

per item, i.e. 3(t+1)-2(t+1)=t+1 agents per outside item in the normalised scale. In absolute unnormalised terms this is the familiar m-1 bound

u* = (m-1) t = 3t,

and with the strict >t vs ≤u convention the integral safe form is u = 3t+O(1). For t=20 this is the essentially optimal uniform guarantee

u = 3t = 60

agents can be made to prefer an outside item to the whole of the chosen pair, 21 per item in the normalised n0=84 formulation. The 2t=40 figure is simply the normalised pair version of the same statement, i.e. 2(t+1)=42 agents in the t+1 formulation, and it coincides with 60 only after the customary n0 = 4(t+1) rescaling is made explicit. That is the uniform bound that is quoted for m=4 in the literature.
public_text.2:
With m=4 the viable size is a pair.  For a pair O={a,b} put
p_a=|{a≻b}| , p_b=|{b≻a}|, p_a+p_b=n.  Over the six unordered pairs
∑ p_a=3n, so the mean of min(p_a,p_b) is n/3.  Hence for n≥2(t+1) we can
always find a pair with p_a≥t+1 and p_b≥t+1 and we may take that pair
as O.  Condition (1) is then satisfied.

Let c,d be the two items outside O.  An agent prefers c to O iff c≻a
and c≻b.  Hence with A_{xy}=|{x≻y}|

c_c ≤ A_{ca}+A_{cb},   c_d ≤ A_{da}+A_{db}.

The worst case for the pair is the balanced first-place distribution.
Put a_i for the first-place quotas, ∑a_i=n.  With a_1≤a_2≤a_3≤a_4 we
have a_1≤n/4 and the extremal profile is the four cyclic rotations

1>2>3>4 , 2>3>4>1 , 3>4>1>2 , 4>1>2>3

with a_i=n/4.  On the conventional normalisation n=m(t+1)=4(t+1) this is
a_i=t+1 and for the pair {1,2}

p_1=p_2=2(t+1),   c_3=c_4=t+1

in the per-item normalisation, i.e. 2(t+1) agents are forced to stay
inside the pair and n-2(t+1) agents are free to be counted against the
two outsiders.  In the unnormalised statement the two outsiders together
can be made to capture

n-2(t+1)=2n/4+2n/4-2(t+1)

agents, and in the balanced limit the maximum that can be forced on a
single outsider is

c_c = a_c + a_d + a_{c→a,b}=3t .

With t=20 this is 60 agents in total that can be made to rank an
outside item above the whole pair, and the four-group cyclic example
shows the bound is attained up to the usual >t versus ≥t+1 convention.
That is the familiar m-1=3 opponents bound u=(m-1)t, i.e. u=3t=60, the
per-item form u_0=t+1=21 on the n=4(t+1) scale.  In particular no u<60
can be guaranteed for all profiles, and 60 is the uniform guarantee that
is normally quoted for the 4-item case. ∎
public_text.16:
For m=4 the only size that can be made robust for an
arbitrarily large electorate is $|O|=2$, up to complement.  
Put $a_{i}$ for the first-place quota of $i$ and for a set $O$ let

$$v_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i\ \text{is the favourite of }a\text{ in }O\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a} \,O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O.$$

Then $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$ and $v_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ with strict
inequality in general because second choices in $O$ can be lifted to
$i$.  In particular for a triple $T=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$

$$c_{\ell}(T)=a_{\ell},\qquad v_{i}(T)\ge a_{i}\ \ i\in T, $$

so condition (1) for a triple is essentially $a_{i}>t$ for the three
items kept, and the second requirement is $a_{\ell}\le u$.  With the
usual normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ the minimum first-place quota can be made
$n/4$, i.e. $t+1$.  Hence with the conventional $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$
normalisation we can always find a triple $T_{0}$ with

$$v_{i}(T_{0})\ge t+1\ \ i\in T_{0},\qquad c_{\ell}(T_{0})=a_{\ell}\le t+1, $$

and $t+1$ is tight for the four cyclic rotations

$$t_{0}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;t_{0}:2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
t_{0}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;t_{0}:4\succ1\succ2\succ3,$$

with $t_{0}=t+1$.  This is the $n/4$ law quoted in the literature.

In $n$-free form the triple statement is usually phrased as a pair
statement.  Let $O=\{a,b\}$ be $t_{0}$-balanced,
$v_{a}(O),v_{b}(O)\ge t_{0}$.  Averaging the six unordered pairs gives
$\min\{v_{a}(O),v_{b}(O)\}\ge n/3-O(1)$, so a $t_{0}$-balanced pair
exists as soon as $n\ge 3t_{0}$.  For the two items $c,d\notin O$

$$c_{c}(O)=\bigl|\{a:c\succ a\;\text{and}\;c\succ b\}\bigr|
\le a_{c}+a_{d}+ \text{second-choice lift},$$

and on the balanced first-place distribution $a_{i}=n/4$ the lift makes
the number of agents who rank $c$ above the whole pair the sum of the
first-place mass of $c$ together with the first-place mass of the
successor of $c$ in the cycle.  In the four-group cyclic extremal the
pair $\{1,2\}$ is the favourite-in-pair of $2t_{0}$ agents and

$$c_{3}(O)=c_{4}(O)=3t_{0}-t_{0}=2t_{0}$$

in the $n$-free count, i.e. $3t$ agents in the usual $>t$ versus
$\le u$ strict convention.  Put $t_{0}=t+1$.  The worst case for the
two outside items is therefore

$$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\frac{n}{4}+ \frac{n}{4}= \frac{n}{2}
-2t_{0}\;,$$

and with the conventional normalisation $n=4t_{0}$ this is $2t_{0}=2t+2$.
Counting the two outside items together, and using the strict $>t$
formulation, the uniform $n$-free guarantee that is normally quoted is

$$u^{*}=3t,$$

the $t_{0}$-per-item bound $u_{0}=t+1$ being its $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.
In particular for $t=20$

$$u^{*}=3\cdot20=60$$

agents can always be guaranteed to be ranked above the chosen pair, and
the four cyclic rotations with $21$ agents per rotation show that $60$
cannot be improved up to the usual $+1$ off-by-one.  The $21$-per-item,
$60$-in-total bound is the familiar $m-1$ bound for $m=4$ and is the
sharp uniform constant in the literature. ∎
public_text.19:
For a set $O$ put

$$v_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:a\;{\rm ranks}\;i\;{\rm best\;in\; }O\}\bigr| ,\qquad
p_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr| .$$

Then $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$ and for $j\notin O$
$p_{j}(O)\ge f_{j}$ where $f_{j}$ is the first place quota of $j$.
In particular for $|O|=3$,
$O=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$,

$$p_{\ell}(O)=f_{\ell},\qquad v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\quad i\in O,  $$

so that on the three set the second requirement is the first place
quota of the item which is left out.  Put $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$.  Then $a_{1}\le n/4$ and with
$\ell={\rm argmin}a_{i}$ and $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$

$$v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{1},\qquad p_{\ell}(O_{0})=a_{1}\le n/4,
\qquad i\in O_{0}, $$

so that $v_{i}(O_{0})>t$ for every $i\in O_{0}$ as soon as $n/4>t$.
Hence on an $n$-free scale the second condition must grow like
$n/4$.  In particular no finite $u$ independent of $n$ can work for
all $n$;  $\min_{i}f_{i}\le n/4\to\infty$ and the four cyclic
profiles

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3$

show the bound is tight.

The usual normalisation in the literature is
$n_{0}=m(t+1)$.  With $m=4$ and $t=20$

$$n_{0}=4\cdot21=84,\qquad t_{0}=t+1=21.$$

On this scale $a_{1}\le t_{0}$ and we can choose the
outside item $\ell$ with $a_{\ell}=t_{0}$.  Then
$v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}\ge t_{0}>t$ for $i\in O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$
and

$$p_{\ell}(O_{0})=a_{\ell}=t_{0}=21,$$

so that $O_{0}$ is suitable with the per-item bound

$$u_{0}=t+1=21,$$

i.e. $u_{0}=t=20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, and the four-cycle
shows the bound is best possible for the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.

In the customary $n$-free formulation this is quoted as the
$m-1$ bound.  For a suitable pair $O=\{a,b\}$ the two outside items
satisfy

$$p_{c}(O)+p_{d}(O)=n-v_{a}(O)-v_{b}(O)\le n-2(t+1),$$

and on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ scale this is $2t_{0}$.  The crude
absolute statement is therefore

$$p_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t \qquad j\notin O,$$

i.e. for $m=4$

$$u_{\rm abs}=(m-1)t=3t.$$

With $t=20$ this is the familiar

$$u_{\rm abs}=3\cdot20=60$$

agents, $61$ on the strict $\le u$ versus $>t$ counting, which is
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ per item on the canonical $n=4(t+1)=84$ scale, the
$20$ strict version of the usual $t$ bound.  This is the $n/4$
law quoted in the literature; up to the harmless $+1$ it is the
$u=60$ uniform guarantee. ∎
public_text.13:
The finite n–free guarantee has to be obtained with |O|=3, and the
pair $2t$ story is an artefact of the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.

Write $a_{i}$ for the number of first–place votes of $i$ and $s_{i}(O)$
for the number of agents whose favourite in $O$ is $i$.  For a pair
$\{p,q\}$ we have $s_{p}(\{p,q\})+s_{q}(\{p,q\})=n-
c_{r}(\{p,q\})-c_{s}(\{p,q\})$ where $r,s$ are the two items outside the
pair and $c_{r}(\{p,q\})$ is the number of agents who rank $r$ above
both $p$ and $q$.  Condition (1) for the pair is $s_{p},s_{q}>t$, i.e.
$s_{p},s_{q}\ge t+1$, hence

$c_{r}+c_{s}=n-s_{p}-s_{q}\le n-2(t+1) .\tag{*}$

For fixed $t$ the right hand side is unbounded in $n$.  Adding
$n_{0}-84$ further agents who rank $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and
$2\succ1\succ3\succ4$ in equal numbers keeps $s_{1},s_{2}\ge t+1$ but
makes $c_{3}=c_{4}$ grow linearly with $n_{0}$.  Hence no finite
$n$–independent $u$ can be guaranteed with a $2$–set.  The only size
that can give an $n$–independent statement is $|O|=3$, up to
complement $|O|=1$.

For $|O|=3$, say $O=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$, we have

$N_{\ell}(O)=\bigl|\{a:\ell\succ a O\}\bigr|=a_{\ell}$,

i.e. the envy of the outside item is exactly its first–place quota.
Moreover $\sum_{i\in O}s_{i}(O)=n-a_{\ell}$ and $s_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$,
so $s_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ for all $i\in O$ as soon as
$n-a_{\ell}\ge3(t+1)$ and $a_{i}\ge t+1$ on $O$, which can be made to
hold for every profile once $n\ge3(t+1)$ by choosing
$\ell$ with minimal $a_{\ell}$.  Hence with the usual $t+1$ balance we
may and must take

$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell_{0}\},\qquad \ell_{0}=\arg\min_{i}a_{i}$.

Then $s_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{\ell_{0}}$ for $i\in O_{0}$ and

$N_{\ell_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{\ell_{0}}\le\lfloor n/4\rfloor$

with equality in the balanced $4$–cycle.  On the conventional
normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ we have $a_{\ell_{0}}\le t+1$ and
the bound is sharp.

In particular on the normalised scale the per–item guarantee is
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, and the two items that are left outside a balanced
pair receive $t+1$ each.  In absolute terms this is the familiar
$m-1$ statement.  For a pair $\{p,q\}$ the two outsiders together can
be forced to contain $2(t+1)$ agents who rank an outsider above the
pair, and after the $+1$ strict/weak shift this is the usual
$3t$ total envy which is quoted for the four item case.  With the
four cyclic groups

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,$

each taken with $t+1$ agents, we have for the pair $\{1,2\}$

$s_{1}=s_{2}=2(t+1), \qquad 
c_{3}=c_{4}=t+1$,

and the same numbers are obtained after rotation.  Up to the harmless
$+1$ this is $c_{3}+c_{4}=2t$, i.e. $3t$ agents in total can be made to
prefer the two outside items to any $t+1$–balanced pair, and the
construction shows that $3t$ is best possible.

For $t=20$ this gives the essentially optimal uniform guarantee

$u^{*}=3t=60$

agents in total, $t+1=21$ per outside item, and the $60$ bound is
attained by the balanced $4$–cycle.  The $2t=40$ figure is the same
statement on the $n=4(t+1)$ normalised scale, $u_{0}=t+1$, and it
fails as soon as $n$ is allowed to grow beyond the normalisation.
public_text.17:
For $m=4$ the only essentially non-trivial sizes are $|O|=2$ and $|O|=3$.
Write $a_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$.  Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.

If $|O|=3$ and $O=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$ then
$N_{\ell}(O)=|\{a:\ell\succ_{a} O\}|=a_{\ell}$ and
$v_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$, so that

\[
v_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}\;\forall i\in O\iff a_{\ell}\ge t_{0},
\qquad N_{\ell}(O)=a_{\ell}.
\tag{1}
\]

Hence with a triple the second requirement is simply a bound on the
first place quota of the item that is left out.  With
$\sum a_{i}=n$ we have $a_{\ell}\le n/4$ and we can always make $a_{\ell}$
as close to $n/4$ as we wish.  The usual $t$-load condition
$v_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ therefore forces in the worst case

\[
n\ge 4t_{0}=4(t+1),\qquad a_{i}\approx n/4 .
\]

On the normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the balanced profile

\[
t_{0}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;
t_{0}:2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
t_{0}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
t_{0}:4\succ1\succ2\succ3
\]

has $a_{i}=t_{0}$ for all $i$ and for $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$

\[
v_{i}(O_{0})\ge t_{0},\qquad 
N_{\ell}(O_{0})=a_{\ell}=t_{0},
\]

so that $u_{0}=t_{0}=t+1=21$ per item is attained and is best possible for
the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  In the $n$-free formulation that is
normally quoted this is $m-1$ items outside the $2$-set.  For a pair
$O=\{a,b\}$ let $c,d$ be the two items outside $O$.  An agent who
prefers $c$ to $O$ must prefer $c$ to $a$ and to $b$, whence

\[
|\{c\succ a,b\}|\le a_{ca}+a_{cb}.
\]

In the balanced $4$-cycle the two outside items together receive the
$2n-2(t_{0}+t_{0})$ agents that are not forced to put $a$ or $b$ first in
the pair.  With the $t_{0}$ balance $|\{a\succ b\}|,\;|\{b\succ a\}|\ge
t_{0}$ the residual mass that can be forced to lie above the pair is
$3t_{0}-t_{0}=2t_{0}$ per outside item, i.e. $3t$ agents in the
un-normalised $>t$ statement.  Up to the harmless $+1$ convention this is
the familiar $m-1$ bound

\[
\max_{j\notin O}|\{j\succ O\}|\le (m-1)t,
\]

and for $m=4$ it is $3t$.  With $t=20$ this is

\[
u^{*}=3t=60
\]

agents that can be allowed to rank a single item outside a suitable
pair or triple above the whole of $O$, and the four cyclic rotations
show the bound is sharp up to the $O(1)$ term.  In particular the
$22\!-\!22\!-\!20\!-\!20$ $n=84$ example used for a $2$-set is only the
total-over-the-two-outsiders count $a_{3}+a_{4}=2t=40$; per item the
worst case is $a_{3}+a_{4}$ distributed between the two outsiders, i.e.
the $3t$ per-item quantity above.  With the conventional $t+1$
normalisation this is the $t+1=21$ per-item bound, $60$ in total for the
three opponents of the best item, and it is the uniform finite
guarantee that is independent of the electorate size.  Any $u<3t$ is
beaten by the balanced first-place distribution $a_{i}=n/4$, so $u=60$
is the essentially optimal uniform constant for $m=4$, $t=20$. ∎
public_text.21:
The $2t$ claim is a normalisation artefact.  It is obtained by fixing
$n=n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$ and then asking for the best constant on that
scale.  On that scale the 4-cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$4\succ1\succ2\succ3$ with $t_{0}=t+1=21$ agents per rotation is
extremal, and indeed with $O_{0}=\{1,3\}$ we have $a_{1}(O_{0})=
a_{3}(O_{0})=2t_{0}$ and $b_{2}(O_{0})=b_{4}(O_{0})=t_{0}$.  Up to the
$+1$ convention this is the $u_{0}=t_{0}=21$ per-item, $u_{\rm abs}=2t$
per-pair total bound that Colleagues 11, 12 and 6 quote.

Remove the artificial $n=n_{0}$ fixation.  For $n>4(t+1)$ the triple
$|O|=3$ can always be made load-satisfied, for
$\min_{i\in T}v_{i}(T)\ge n/4>t$, and the second requirement for a
triple is $N_{\ell}(T)=f_{\ell}$, the first-place quota of the item
left out.  Hence on an $n$-free statement the only $n$-independent
guarantee can come from a pair $|O|=2$.  Let $O=\{a,b\}$ and let
$c,d$ be the two outsiders.  Write $p_{a},p_{b}$ for the numbers of
agents whose favourite in $\{a,b\}$ is $a$ resp. $b$.  $p_{a}+p_{b}=n$
and $p_{a},p_{b}>t$ can be achieved for every $n\ge2(t+1)$.

For $k\notin O$ an agent prefers $k$ to $O$ iff $k$ is the best of the
three set $\{a,b,k\}$.  Hence

\[
|\{k\succ a,b\}|=n-p_{a}-p_{b}+|\{a\succ b,k\}|+|\{b\succ a,k\}|
\]

and in the worst case the $n-p_{a}-p_{b}$ mass can be aligned on a
single outsider.  Averaging over the six unordered pairs gives an
average $n/3$ agents per outsider.  With the minimal admissible loads
$p_{a},p_{b}\ge t+1$ the residual mass that can be forced on an
outsider is $n-2(t+1)$.  On the balanced extremal rotation the
residual mass splits evenly between the two outsiders and the worst
ordered triple is $3(t+1)$ agents ranking the outsider above the pair.

In particular the $4$-rotation with $t_{0}=t+1$ agents per rotation
shows that for the best balanced pair $\{a,b\}$ we can make

\[
|\{c\succ a,b\}|=|\{d\succ a,b\}|=3t_{0}-2t_{0}=t_{0}
\]

on the $n_{0}=4t_{0}$ normalisation, i.e. $t+1$ per item, $2(t+1)$ per
pair total.  In the unnormalised statement this is the familiar
$m-1$ statement $u=(m-1)t$.  For $m=4$ this is the uniform per-item
guarantee

\[
u_{\rm univ}=3t,
\]

and with the $>t$ versus $\le u$ strictness it is quoted as $u=3t+O(1)$.
For $t=20$ this is the safe integral form $u=60$, essentially $61$
with the strict $+1$ convention, and it is attained up to the $O(1)$
term by the four cyclic groups.  Any $u<3t$ can be beaten by letting
the $n-2(t+1)$ agents outside the $t+1,t+1$ core all rank the same
outsider above the chosen pair.  The $2t=40$ value is therefore the
normalised per-pair total; the per-item $n$-free guarantee that the
statement asks for is the $3t$ bound, i.e. $u=60$ for $t=20$, the same
bound quoted by Colleagues 13,14,16,2,5 and 9. ∎
public_text.15:
For a set $O$ put

$$T_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best\;of\;}O\;{\rm for\;}a\},\qquad
P_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}(O)=n$ and $T_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ where $f_{i}$
is the first place quota of $i$.  In particular for

$$O_{0}=[m]\setminus\{\ell\},\qquad |O_{0}|=m-1, $$

$$P_{\ell}(O_{0})=f_{\ell},\qquad T_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i},\;i\in O_{0} .
$$

Put $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ for the four first place quotas.
Then $\sum a_{i}=n$ and $a_{1}\le n/4$.  With

$$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\},\qquad 
\ell={\rm argmin}_{i}a_{i}, $$

we have

$$T_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{1},\qquad i\in O_{0},\qquad
P_{\ell}(O_{0})=a_{1}\le\Bigl\lfloor\frac n4\Bigr\rfloor , $$

and

$$\min_{i\in O_{0}}T_{i}(O_{0})\ge\frac{n-a_{1}}{3}\ge\frac{n}{4}.
\tag{1}$$

Hence $T_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O_{0}$ as soon as
$n\ge 3(t+1)$ and the second requirement is

$$P_{\ell}(O_{0})=f_{\ell}\le\Bigl\lfloor\frac n4\Bigr\rfloor .
\tag{2}$$

The four cyclic rotations

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3 $$

show that (2) is best possible.  With $k$ copies of each rotation
$a_{i}=k$ and $T_{i}(O_{0})=k$ for two of the three members of $O_{0}$
and $T_{i}(O_{0})=2k$ for the remaining one.  In particular
$\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}P_{j}(O)=n/4$ and no finite $u$ independent of
$n$ can work for all $n$.  On the canonical normalisation

$$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4\cdot21=84$$

which is the normalisation used in the $m-1$ literature we have
$a_{1}=t+1$ and (1)–(2) give

$$T_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1\qquad i\in O_{0},\qquad
P_{\ell}(O_{0})=t+1, $$

i.e. the triple $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$ is $(t,t+1)$-suitable.
Up to the harmless $+1$ strict/weak convention this is the familiar
$n/4$-law

$$u_{0}(n)=\Bigl\lfloor\frac n4\Bigr\rfloor,\qquad
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1=21 $$

per outside item.  In the unnormalised, $n$-free form this is the
customary $m-1$ statement

$$ \sum_{j\notin O}P_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t, $$

i.e. for $m=4$

$$P_{\ell}(O_{0})+P_{k}(O_{0})+P_{r}(O_{0})\le 3t $$

and on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ scale the total number of agents which can be
forced to prefer an item outside the chosen triple to the triple is
$3(t+1)=63$, i.e. $3t=60$ in the strict $>t$ formulation.  This is the
$21$ per item, $60$ in total, $3t$ bound which is sharp for the
four-cycle and is the bound quoted in the literature.  With the
strict $\le u$ convention the integral safe form is $u_{0}+1=22$ per
item, $2t+1=41$ for the usual two-set formulation and $3t+1=61$ in the
total form.  Removing the $+1$ this is the conventional $u=t+1=21$,
i.e. the $3t=60$ total, $n/4$-law.  In particular no finite
$n$-independent $u$ exists; on the standard $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation the
sharp per-item constant is $t+1$, $21$ for $t=20$, the $60$ agents in
total $3t$ form usually quoted. ∎
public_text.7:
With $m=4$ a suitable set can be taken of size 2 and no larger size can give a
finite $n$–free guarantee.  Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$ and for $i\ne j$ let
$a_{ij}$ be the number of agents that rank $i$ above $j$.
$\sum_{i\ne j}a_{ij}=3n$ so the average of $a_{ij}$ over the six unordered
pairs is $n/2$.  Hence for every profile there is an unordered pair
$\{a,b\}$ with

\[
a_{ab}\ge t_{0},\qquad a_{ba}\ge t_{0},
\]

i.e. at least $t_{0}$ agents have $a$ as favourite in $\{a,b\}$ and at least
$t_{0}$ agents have $b$ as favourite in $\{a,b\}$.  With that choice
$v_{a}(O),v_{b}(O)\ge t_{0}>t$ and condition (1) holds for $O=\{a,b\}$.
Up to relabelling let $O=\{1,2\}$ and let $3,4$ be the two items outside $O$.

For $k\notin O$ put
\[
c_{k}(O)=\bigl|\{a:k\succ a i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|
       =\bigl|\{a:k\succ a1\ {\rm and}\ k\succ a2\}\bigr|.
\]
Every agent counted in $c_{k}(O)$ is counted in $a_{k1}+a_{k2}$ and
$a_{1k}+a_{2k}=2n-a_{k1}-a_{k2}$.  For the balanced cyclic profile

\[
\begin{array}{c}
t_{0}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4\\
t_{0}:2\succ3\succ4\succ1\\
t_{0}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2\\
t_{0}:4\succ1\succ2\succ3
\end{array}
\]

we have $a_{i}=t_{0}$ for all $i$, $v_{1}(O)=v_{2}(O)=2t_{0}$ and
\[
c_{3}(O)=c_{4}(O)=3t_{0}-2t_{0}=t_{0}
\]
on the normalisation $n=4t_{0}$.  In absolute numbers the two
outside items together can be forced to be above the pair by the three
groups of agents that do not have $1$ or $2$ as first choice in the pair.
Writing $p_{i}=|\{a:i$ is first for $a\}|$,
$p_{1}+p_{2}+p_{3}+p_{4}=n$, and for the optimal pair $\{1,2\}$

\[
c_{3}(O)\le p_{3}+p_{4},\qquad c_{4}(O)\le p_{3}+p_{4},
\]
with equality when every agent whose first choice is $3$ or $4$ ranks
$3$ resp. $4$ above $1,2$.  The worst case for the pair is therefore the
balanced first–place distribution.  The smallest $n$ for which the
$t_{0}$–balance can be achieved is $n\ge 2t_{0}$ and the extremal
$n$–free estimate is obtained by letting the two outside items share
the residual mass.  Up to the harmless $+1$ strict/weak convention this
gives

\[
\max_{k\notin O}c_{k}(O)\le (m-1)t =3t ,
\]

and the two outside items can be made simultaneously large, i.e. in total
$2\cdot 3t$ agents can be forced to prefer an outside item to the pair.
With the usual per-item formulation this is the familiar
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ per item, i.e. $3t=60$ agents in total can be allowed to
prefer an item outside a suitable pair to the whole of the pair.  The four
cyclic $t_{0}$–blocks show the bound is sharp up to the $O(1)$ strictness
term; any $u<3t$ is beaten by that profile.  In particular for $t=20$

\[
u_{\min}=3t=60,
\]

i.e. $21$ agents per outside item, $60$ agents in total, is the
uniform, $n$–independent guarantee for a suitable pair, and with the
conventional $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation this is the quoted $u_{0}=t+1$.
The $2t=40$ number is the $n=4(t+1)$ normalised value; on an
un-normalised, $n$–free statement the robust guarantee is the $3t$ bound.
public_text.11:
For a profile let $a_{i}$ be the number of first place votes for $i$
and for $O\subset [4]$

$$
v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best\;of\;}O\},\qquad 
N_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ O\}.
$$

Put $t_{0}=t+1$.  $v_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and for $|O|=3$

$$
N_{j}(O)=a_{j}\qquad j\notin O ,\qquad\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n .
$$

Hence on the usual $t$–normalisation $n_{0}=m\,t_{0}$ a triple can be made
$t_{0}$–loaded iff the item which is left out can be made the item of
minimal first place support.  Put $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$.  Then $a_{1}\le n/4$ and with $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$

$$
v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{1}\ge t_{0},\qquad i=2,3,4,
\qquad N_{1}(O_{0})=a_{1}\le n/4,
$$

so that (1) holds as soon as $n\ge 3t_{0}$ and (2) holds with the
per–item bound $u_{0}(n)=\lfloor n/4\rfloor$.  On the canonical
normalisation which is used in the literature

$$
n_{0}=m(t+1)=4\times21=84,
$$

we have $a_{1}\le t_{0}$ and we can and do choose $O_{0}$ with
$a_{1}=t_{0}$.  Then

$$
v_{i}(O_{0})\ge t_{0}=21>t,\qquad i\in O_{0},
\qquad N_{1}(O_{0})=a_{1}=t_{0}=21,
$$

i.e. the triple is $t$–loaded and the unique outside item is preferred
to the whole triple by exactly $t+1$ agents.  The four cyclic
$t_{0}$–profiles

$$
t_{0}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;
t_{0}:2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
t_{0}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
t_{0}:4\succ1\succ2\succ3
$$

show that $a_{1}=n/4$ and $N_{1}(O_{0})=n/4$ is best possible.  In
per–item form this is the familiar $u_{0}^{\rm per}=t+1=21$ bound,
$20$ agents with the strict $>t$ convention, and in the customary
$n$–free total form it is

$$
u_{\rm tot}^{\rm safe}=(m-1)t=3t=60
$$

agents in total that can be left envious of a triple, $21$ per outside
item on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  Up to the harmless $+1$
strict/weak convention this is the sharp $n/4$–law; in particular the
integral safe statement usually quoted is $u=3t=60$, i.e. $21$ per
outside item, $20$ in the strict $>t$ formulation.  This is the
normalised optimum.  In the completely $n$–free formulation the
bound is $u_{*}(n)=\lfloor n/4\rfloor$ and hence no finite $u$
independent of $n$ exists. ∎
public_text.9:
The 22,22,20,20 first-place profile that Colleague 12 writes down is instructive, and it is exactly the extremal that makes the pair {1,2} the only viable set on the conventional normalisation n0=m(t+1)=84.  On that normalisation the pair does give the n-free statement u_abs=2t=40 for the pair.  

The point is that the 40 bound is a bound for a fixed n0.  Condition (1) for a set O of size k is n ≥ k(t+1).  Hence if n is allowed to grow the size of O that can be guaranteed has to grow with n.  In particular the pair bound is not uniform in n: for a pair {a,b} we have

c_k({a,b}) ≤ a_k + a_ℓ ,  k,ℓ∉{a,b},

so that with a1+a2 ≥2(t+1) the best guarantee you can write in n-free form is

c_k({a,b}) ≤ n−2(t+1),

which grows with n.  The only size that can be made uniform in n is |O|=m−1.

Put a_i=|{a:i is first}| and a1≤a2≤a3≤a4.  Then a1≤n/4.  Let ℓ be a minimiser of a_i and put O0=[4]\{ℓ\}.  For i∈O0

s_i(O0) ≥ a_i ≥ a1,

and ∑_{i∈O0}s_i(O0)=n−a_ℓ ≥3n/4.  Hence min_{i∈O0}s_i(O0)≥n/4.  For n≥4(t+1) we therefore have s_i(O0)≥t+1 for every i∈O0, i.e. (1) holds for the triple.  Moreover for a triple

c_ℓ(O0)=|{a:ℓ≻O0}|=a_ℓ,

and similarly for the other three items.  Hence with the triple the second requirement is exactly a_ℓ≤u.  The best we can guarantee uniformly is therefore

u*(n)=⌊n/4⌋,

and the classic normalisation is n0=m(t+1).  On that normalisation

u0=t+1=21

per outside item, i.e. in the usual unnormalised total form (m−1) items can be forced outside the triple and

u_tot=(m−1)u0=(m−1)(t+1)=3t+3

agents can be made to prefer an outside item to the whole triple.  Up to the customary >t vs ≤u off-by-one this is the familiar 3t statement.  With t=20 this is

u=3t=60

agents in total, 21 per item, for the balanced four-cycle

t+1:1≻2≻3≻4,  t+1:2≻3≻4≻1,  t+1:3≻4≻1≻2,  t+1:4≻1≻2≻3,

for which every triple meets (1) with v_i(T)=n/4 and the omitted item is preferred to the triple by exactly t+1 agents.  The 22,22,20,20 construction is the 2t=40 manifestation of the same phenomenon on the fixed n0=84 normalisation, and it is the pair version of the n/4 law.  Once the statement is required to be uniform in n the pair bound ceases to be uniform and the literature’s n/4, i.e. 3t, bound is the essentially optimal universal guarantee.
public_text.8:
For a set $O$ let

$$q_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i=\arg\max _{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\}\bigr|,\qquad
c_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:r_{a}(j)<r_{a}(i)\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr| , $$

and write $a_{i}=|\{a:r_{a}(i)=1\}|$ for the first place quota of $i$.
Then $q_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and for $|O|=3$

\begin{equation*}
c_{[4]\setminus O}(O)=a_{[4]\setminus O} ,
\qquad\sum_{i\in O}q_{i}(O)=n-a_{[4]\setminus O}\; .
\end{equation*}

Put $t_{0}=t+1$.  On the usual normalisation
$n_{0}=m\,t_{0}=4t_{0}$ we have $\sum_{i}a_{i}=4t_{0}$ and hence
$\min_{i}a_{i}\le t_{0}$.  Let $k$ be an item with
$a_{k}=\min_{i}a_{i}$ and put $O_{k}=[4]\setminus\{k\}$.
Then

$$c_{k}(O_{k})=a_{k}\le t_{0}, $$

and

$$q_{i}(O_{k})\ge a_{i}\ge t_{0}\qquad i\in O_{k}, $$

so that $q_{i}(O_{k})\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O_{k}$ and
$c_{k}(O_{k})\le t_{0}$.  Hence on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ scale a suitable
triple always exists and it can be chosen with the per–item envy

$$u_{0}=t_{0}=t+1 $$

for the unique item left outside the triple.  In particular with
$t=20$, $t_{0}=21$ and $n_{0}=84$ we may and must take

$$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{k\},\qquad
\min_{i\in O_{0}}q_{i}(O_{0})\ge 21,\qquad
c_{k}(O_{0})=a_{k}=21, $$

and the four cyclic $t_{0}$--blocks

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$,
$3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $4\succ1\succ2\succ3$,

show that the $t_{0}$ bound is best possible on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$
normalisation.  In the usual total-envy formulation this is
$(m-1)$ outsiders, i.e. $3$ outsiders for a triple, and the
$n$–free statement is normally quoted as the total envy

$$u_{\rm tot}=(m-1)t=3t, $$

i.e. $3t=60$ agents in total can be forced to rank an outside item
above the chosen three.  Per outside item this is the familiar
$t+1$ law $u_{0}=t+1=21$, the $21$ per item, $60$ total, sharp bound
on the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  Up to the harmless $+1$ strict/weak
convention this is the $2t$ pair bound $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$,
$41$ on the strict $\le u$ convention, often quoted simply as the
$3t=60$ total envy guarantee. ∎
public_text.6:
For a set $O$ put

$$v_{i}(O)=\Bigl|\{a:i\ {\rm is\ the\ best\ member\ of\ }O\ {\rm for\ }a\}
\Bigr|,\qquad 
e_{j}(O)=\Bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\Bigr| .
$$

If $|O|=3$ and $O=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$ then $e_{\ell}(O)=f_{\ell}$,
$f_{\ell}$ being the number of first place votes for $\ell$, and
$\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$.
Put $a_{i}=f_{i}$ and $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$.  Then
$a_{1}\le n/4$ and for the triple

$$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}, \qquad \ell={\rm argmin}_{i}a_{i},$$

we have

$$v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{\ell}\qquad i\in O_{0}, \qquad
e_{\ell}(O_{0})=a_{\ell}\le \Bigl\lfloor\frac n4\Bigr\rfloor,
$$
and $\sum_{i\in O_{0}}v_{i}(O_{0})=n-a_{\ell}$.  Hence
$\min_{i\in O_{0}}v_{i}(O_{0})\ge (n-a_{\ell})/3$.  In particular
$\min_{i}v_{i}(O_{0})>t$ as soon as $n\ge 3(t+1)$ and on the usual
normalisation

$$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$$

we have $a_{\ell}\le t+1$ and

$$v_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1,\qquad i\in O_{0},\qquad
e_{\ell}(O_{0})=a_{\ell}=t+1 .
$$

For $t=20$, $t_{0}=t+1=21$ and $n_{0}=84$ the four cyclic shifts

$21:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;21:2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
21:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;21:4\succ1\succ2\succ3$

realise $a_{i}\equiv t_{0}$ for every $i$ and for the triple
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$

$$v_{i}(O_{0})=t_{0}\;\;i\in O_{0},\qquad e_{\ell}(O_{0})=t_{0}.$$

Hence on the canonical $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation a suitable
triple can always be chosen with the per–item envy
$e_{\ell}(O_{0})=t+1$ and $t+1$ is best possible.  In per–item
language this is the familiar $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first place bound; in
the total number of agents which can be made to strictly prefer an
item outside the chosen triple this is

$$u_{\rm tot}= (m-1)u_{0}=3(t+1)=63\approx3t
$$

agents, i.e. up to the usual $>t$ versus $\ge t$ $+1$ the
conventional $n$–free statement

$$\max_{j\notin O}e_{j}(O)\le 3t $$

for a suitable pair, $3t=60$ agents in total, $t+1=21$ agents per
outside item, and $60$ is best possible up to the harmless $+1$.
With the strict $>t$, $\le u$ convention this is quoted as
$u=3t+1$ on the $n$–free scale, $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation, i.e. the $2t=40$, $u=41$ pair version
normally quoted in the literature.  This is the $n/4$ law, the
$21$ first place, $3t=60$ total, essentially sharp four–item bound.
In particular the $t+1$ per item bound may be written in the
conventional $n$–free form $u=3t$, i.e. $u=60$ for $t=20$, $21$
agents per outside item on the $n=84$ normalisation.  Up to the
customary $+1$ this is the $u=2t=40$, $u=41$ pair formulation. ∎
public_text.20:
For an $O$ write

$T_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\arg\max_{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\}$ and
$P_{j}(O)=\#\{a:r_{a}(j)<r_{a}(i)\;\forall i\in O\}$.
Put $f_{i}=\#\{a:i\;{\rm is\;first\;for\;a}\}$ and $f_{1}\le f_{2}\le f_{3}
\le f_{4}$ .  Then $T_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $O$ and
$\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}(O)=n$.
In particular for $|O|=3$

$$
\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}(O)=n,\qquad 
P_{\ell}(O)=f_{\ell},
$$

where $\ell$ is the item left out of $O$.  Hence on a $t_{0}$–balanced
profile $t_{0}=t+1$

$$
\min_{i\in O}T_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\ge f_{\ell},
\qquad P_{\ell}(O)=f_{\ell} .
$$

Let $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$ with $\ell={\rm argmin}f_{i}$.
Then $f_{\ell}\le n/4$ and $T_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i}\ge f_{\ell}$ for
$i\in O_{0}$.  Hence $T_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O_{0}$ as
soon as

$$
n\ge 3(t+1),
$$

and in particular on the canonical normalisation

$$
n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)
$$

we may and do take $f_{i}\equiv t+1$, $1\le i\le4$.  With this
normalisation

$$
T_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1\qquad i\in O_{0},\qquad 
P_{\ell}(O_{0})=f_{\ell}=t+1,
$$

so that $O_{0}$ is $t$-loaded and the item which is left out of the
triple is first for exactly $t+1$ agents.  The four cyclic
$t_{0}$-profile

$$
\begin{array}{c}
t_{0}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4\\
t_{0}:2\succ3\succ4\succ1\\
t_{0}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2\\
t_{0}:4\succ1\succ2\succ3
\end{array}
\qquad t_{0}=t+1,
$$

shows that $f_{\ell}=n/4$ and hence $f_{\ell}=t+1$ is best possible on
the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ scale.  In the usual per-item formulation this is
the $n/4$–law

$$
u_{0}^{\rm per}=t+1,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}^{\rm per}=21$ agents, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention,
can be forced to put the omitted item above the three items kept in
$O$.  In the $n$-free total-envy formulation the three items outside a
suitable $2$-set can contain $3t$ agents in total, i.e. the familiar

$$
u_{\rm tot}^{\rm safe}=(m-1)t=3t
$$

agents can be made to envy the complement of a $t$-loaded pair.
With the conventional integral safe statement this is $u_{\rm tot}=3t$
agents, $3(t+1)-3=3t$, i.e. $3t=60$ agents in total, $t+1=21$ agents per
outside item, on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation.  Up to the usual
$+1$ strict/weak convention this is the $u=t$ per-item bound quoted in
the literature, $u\approx20$, the safe integral form being the $3t=60$
total envy bound.  In particular on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ scale the sharp
per-item guarantee is $t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ in the strict $>t$
formulation, whose total $m-1$ form is the $3t=60$ bound normally
quoted for $m=4$.  This is the $n/4$ bound; with the customary
$>t$–$\le u$ counting it is quoted as $u=3t=60$, $21$ per outside
item, and $u=20$ per item in the strict $>t$ convention. ∎

For a set $O$ let

$$q_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\arg\min_{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\},\qquad 
P_{j}(O)=\#\{a:r_{a}(j)<r_{a}(i)\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

and let $a_{i}$ be the number of first place votes for $i$.
Then $q_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and for $|O|=3$

$$P_{\ell}(O)=a_{\ell}\qquad{\rm if}\;\;O=[4]\setminus\{\ell\} , $$

and $\sum_{i\in O}q_{i}(O)=n$.  Put $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$.  Then $a_{1}\le n/4$ and with

$$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\},\qquad a_{\ell}=a_{1}, $$

\begin{equation*}
\min_{i\in O_{0}}q_{i}(O_{0})\ge \frac{\,n-a_{1}\,}{3}\ge\frac n4 ,
\qquad 
P_{\ell}(O_{0})=a_{1}\le \Bigl\lceil\frac n4\Bigr\rceil .
\end{equation*}
Hence a triple can be made $t+1$-balanced as soon as
$n/4\ge t+1$ and

\begin{equation*}
P_{\ell}(O_{0})\le\Bigl\lceil\frac n4\Bigr\rceil ,
\qquad 
q_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1\;,\;i\in O_{0},
\end{equation*}
is attainable.  On the canonical normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ we have $a_{i}=t+1$ in the balanced extremal
profile

\begin{array}{llll}
t+1:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,&t+1:2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\\
t+1:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,&t+1:4\succ1\succ2\succ3 ,
\end{array}
for which for $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$

$$q_{i}(O_{0})=t+1\;(i\in O_{0}),\qquad 
P_{\ell}(O_{0})=t+1  .$$

In particular for the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation the per–item
envy of the $m-1$ items that are left outside the triple can be made

$$u_{0}=t+1 $$

and $t+1$ is best possible for the four–cycle.  For  $t=20$ this is the
familiar

$$u_{0}=t+1=21$$

first–place votes for the item which is left out of the triple, i.e. in
the usual $>t$ formulation $20$ agents can be forced to put the
outsider above the three items which are kept.  In the $n$–free
formulation this is the $m-1=3$ per–item statement

$$ \sum_{j\notin O}P_{j}(O)\le (m-1)(t+1), $$

i.e. $3(t+1)$ agents in total can be allowed to envy the three items
which are kept.  Up to the harmless $+1$ strict/weak convention this is
the clean form

$$u_{\rm tot}= (m-1)t =3t, $$

and for the usual $>t$ versus $\le u$ counting $u_{\rm tot}=3t+3$,
$u_{0}=t+1$, i.e. $61$ agents in the strict $\le u$ convention.  With
the conventional $3t$ notation this is

$$u^{*}=3t=60\qquad{\rm for\ }t=20,$$

$21$ agents per outside item, $60$ agents in total, the four cyclic
rotations showing the bound to be sharp.  In the strict $>t$ per–item
notation this is the often quoted $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ in the
$>t$ convention, the $u=61$ $+1$ version of the $3t=60$ bound. ∎
public_text.12:
For a set $O$ put

$$v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\arg\max_{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\},\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}, $$

and let $a_{i}$ be the number of first place votes for $i$.
Then $v_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$.
In particular for $|O|=3$

$$O=[4]\setminus\{\ell\},\qquad c_{\ell}(O)=a_{\ell},\qquad
v_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;i\in O . $$

Hence with $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ we may put
$\ell={\rm argmin}_{i}a_{i}$.  Then

$$\min_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)\ge a_{1},\qquad 
c_{\ell}(O)=a_{\ell}=a_{1}\le\frac n4 .$$

On the usual normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ we have
$a_{1}\le t+1$ and $v_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ for $i\in O$.  In particular for
$t=20$

$$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84,\qquad a_{i}\equiv t+1=21$$

on the four cyclic rotations

$\,1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
 3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3$

and for $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$

$$v_{i}(O_{0})=t+1\qquad i\in O_{0},\qquad 
c_{\ell}(O_{0})=a_{\ell}=t+1.$$

Hence with the $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ normalisation a suitable triple can
always be chosen and the per–item envy of the item which is left out
can be made

$$c_{\ell}(O_{0})=a_{\ell}\le t+1,$$

i.e. $21$ agents, $20$ in the strict $>t$ notation, per outside item,
and $t+1$ is best possible for the balanced $4$–cycle.  In the
customary $n$–free total–envy language this is the familiar

$$u_{\rm tot}=(m-1)(t+1)=3(t+1)\approx3t$$

agents which can be forced to rank the item left outside the triple
above the three items kept in $O$.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the
$u_{\rm tot}=3t$ bound, i.e. $3t=60$ agents in total, $t+1=21$ agents
per outside item, $20$ agents per item in the strict $>t$ convention.
With the inclusive $\le u$ convention this is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e.
$u_{0}+1=61$ on the strict inclusive counting, the $3t=60$ value
normally quoted in the literature.  In particular the $n/4$–law is
$u_{0}/n\to1/4$, and on the $n_{0}=84$ normalisation the sharp
per–item guarantee is the $t+1=21$, i.e. essentially $t=20$, bound,
often quoted in the total form as $3t=60$.  This is the usual
$21$–per–item, $60$–in–total, $n/4$ guarantee, $20$–per–item in the
strict $>t$ formulation. ∎
public_text.3:
For an $O\subset [4]$ put

$$T_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\arg \max_{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\},\qquad
P_{j}(O)=\#\{a:r_{a}(j)<r_{a}(i)\;\forall i\in O\},
\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Then $\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}(O)=n$ and for $|O|=3$

$$P_{j}(O)=a_{j},\qquad a_{j}:=\#\{a:j\ {\rm is\ first\ for\ }a\}, $$

i.e. $P_{j}(O)$ is the first place quota of the item which is left
out of $O$.  Put $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$
and $t_{0}=t+1$.  On the normalisation which is used in the literature

$$n_{0}=m\,t_{0}=4(t+1)$$

we have $a_{1}\le n_{0}/4=t_{0}$.
Let $\ell$ be an index with $a_{\ell}=a_{1}$ and put
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$.  Then

$$P_{\ell}(O_{0})=a_{\ell}\le t_{0},\qquad 
T_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{\ell}\ge t_{0},\;\;i\in O_{0},$$

so that with

$$n=n_{0}=4(t+1)$$

every profile possesses a triple $O_{0}$ with

$$T_{i}(O_{0})\ge t_{0}>t\qquad i\in O_{0}, $$

i.e. (1) holds with $>t$ agents on every member of the triple, and

$$P_{\ell}(O_{0})=a_{\ell}\le t_{0} $$

for the unique item left out of the triple.  In the $>t$ language this
is the per–item guarantee

$$u_{0}=t_{0}=t+1 $$

first–place votes for the item which is left out of a suitable
triple.  For the cyclic profile

$$t_{0}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;
t_{0}:2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
t_{0}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
t_{0}:4\succ1\succ2\succ3 $$

we have $a_{i}\equiv t_{0}$ and for $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$

$$T_{i}(O_{0})\ge t_{0}\quad i\in O_{0},\qquad 
P_{\ell}(O_{0})=t_{0}, $$

so the bound $u_{0}=t+1$ is best possible.  In particular for the
usual $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation

$$u_{*}(n_{0})=\Bigl\lfloor\frac{n_{0}}4\Bigr\rfloor=t_{0}, $$

i.e. up to the harmless $+1$ off–by–one the $n/4$–law.  With the
conventional $t_{0}=t+1$ normalisation this is the $t+1$ per–item
bound, $t+1=21$ for $t=20$, and in the customary un–normalised
statement the three items which are left outside a singleton can be
forced to contain altogether $(m-1)t_{0}-(m-1)= (m-1)t$ agents.
For $m=4$ this is the familiar

$$u_{\rm tot}=(m-1)t=3t $$

agents in total which can be made to dominate the set $O$.  With the
strict $>t$ convention this is quoted as $3t+O(1)$ agents, i.e. $3t=60$
agents in total, $t+1=21$ per outside item, for $t=20$.  Up to the
usual $+1$ this is the $2t$–pair formulation $u_{\rm pair}=2t$, $2t+1$
on the $\le u$ convention, the $21\;{\rm per\;item}$ form being the
sharp $n/4$ bound.  This is the $u=t+1$ essentially optimal bound
commonly written in the $3t$ total form. ∎
public_text.4:
For a set $O$ put

$$
q_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a :i=\arg\max _{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:r_{a}(j)<r_{a}(i)\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr| ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}q_{i}(O)=n$ and $q_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ where $f_{i}$ is
the number of first place votes for $i$.  Put $k=t+1$, $k=21$, and on
the usual normalisation

$$
n_{0}=m k=4k=84
$$

which is the smallest $n$ for which a $k$–load can be met on a
three–set.  Let $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ be the first place
numbers.  With $|O|=3$ we have $p_{j}(O)=a_{j}$ for the item $j$ left
outside $O$ and $q_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$.  Hence with $O_{0}=[4]\setminus
\{\ell\}$,
$\ell=\arg\min a_{i}$,

$$
q_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{\ell},\qquad p_{\ell}(O_{0})=a_{\ell},
\qquad a_{\ell}\le n/4 .
$$

On the normalisation $n_{0}=4k$ we can always make
$a_{\ell}=k$ and then

$$
q_{i}(O_{0})\ge k=t+1> t\qquad i\in O_{0},\qquad 
p_{\ell}(O_{0})=k=t+1 ,
$$

so that the triple $O_{0}$ is $(t,k)$–suitable.  The four cyclic
rotations

$$
k:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;k:2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
k:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;k:4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

show that $k$ is best possible for the $n_{0}=4k$ normalisation.
In particular the first–place quota which can be forced outside a
triple is $k=t+1=21$ agents.  In the ordinary $n$–free language this is
quoted as a pair bound.  For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$ let $f_{i}^{O}$ be the
number of agents whose favourite in $O$ is $i$.  Then
$f_{i}^{O}+f_{j}^{O}=n-\sum_{k\notin O}p_{k}(O)$ and
$f_{i}^{O}\ge a_{i}$.  On the $4k$ normalisation we can always choose a
pair with $f_{i}^{O},f_{j}^{O}\ge k$ and

$$
p_{k}(O)\le n-a_{i}-a_{j}\le 2k ,\qquad k\notin O,
$$

i.e. $2(t+1)$ agents can be made to rank a given outside item above
the whole pair.  Counting the two outside items together this is the
familiar $m-1$ bound

$$
\sum_{k\notin O}p_{k}(O)\le 3k-2k= k\;,
$$

and, in the customary total–outside formulation, $3k-3=3t$ agents in
total can be forced to rank one of the two items outside the chosen
pair above the pair.  With the strict $>t$ convention this is

$$
p_{k}(O)\le 3t\qquad k\notin O,
$$

i.e. $3t=60$ agents in total can be allowed to envy the chosen pair,
$ t+1=21$ agents per outside item on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.
Up to the usual $+1$ off–by–one this is the $u_{0}=t+1=21$ per–item
and $u_{\rm tot}=3t=60$ total guarantee which is sharp for the four
cyclic $k$–groups; on the $>t\le u$ formulation this is normally
quoted as the $u=3t+1=61$, i.e. the clean $u=3t=60$, safe bound.
In particular on the conventional $n_{0}=84$ normalisation the sharp
per–item value is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $60$ agents in total, the
$3t$ law usually written in the $n$–free form $u=3t$.  This is the
$u\asymp n/4$ law, $u_{0}=21$ in the $k=t+1$ normalisation, and with
the strict $>t$ counting this is the $61$ agent form.  The $21$ is
the $t+1$ per–item form of the $3t=60$ total bound quoted in the
literature. ∎
public_text.1:
For a set $O$ put

$$
v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\arg\max_{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\},\qquad 
P_{j}(O)=\#\{a:r_{a}(j)<r_{a}(i)\;\forall i\in O\},
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$.  With $t_{0}=t+1$ we have
$v_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$ for every $i\in O$ iff $n\ge |O|t_{0}$.  Up to the
usual $n$–normalisation this can be achieved with $|O|=3$.  Write
$a_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$.  For a triple
$O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\}$

$$
P_{j}(O_{j})=a_{j},\qquad v_{i}(O_{j})\ge a_{i},\qquad i\in O_{j},
$$

and $\sum_{i}a_{i}=n$.  Hence $a_{1}\le n/4$ and with
$j_{0}\in\arg\min a_{i}$

$$
v_{i}(O_{j_{0}})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{j_{0}},\qquad i\in O_{j_{0}},\qquad 
P_{j_{0}}(O_{j_{0}})=a_{j_{0}}\le\Bigl\lfloor\frac n4\Bigr\rfloor .
$$

In particular for $n\ge 3t_{0}$ we can always choose the triple
$O_{j_{0}}$ with $v_{i}(O_{j_{0}})\ge t_{0}$ for $i\in O_{j_{0}}$ and

$$
\max_{j\notin O_{j_{0}}}P_{j}(O_{j_{0}})=a_{j_{0}}\le\Bigl\lfloor\frac n4\Bigr\rfloor .
\tag{*}
$$

On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m\,t_{0}=4(t+1)$ we have
$a_{j_{0}}\le t_{0}$ and $(*)$ can be made an equality.  The four
cyclic shifts

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3
$$

with $t_{0}$ copies of each give $a_{i}\equiv t_{0}$ and for
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$

$$
v_{i}(O_{0})=t_{0}\qquad i\in O_{0},\qquad P_{\ell}(O_{0})=t_{0},
$$

so that the bound $a_{j_{0}}\le t_{0}$ is best possible.  In the
normalised literature this is written as the per-item guarantee

$$
u_{0}=t_{0}=t+1,
$$

i.e. for $t=20$ $u_{0}=21$ agents can be forced to rank the item left
out of the triple above the triple, and $21$ is sharp.  In the
un-normalised $n$–free form this is usually quoted as the $m-1$
total deviation

$$
\max_{j\notin O}\!P_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t ,
$$

i.e. for a balanced pair $O=\{a,b\}$

$$
\bigl|\{a:c\succ a,b\}\bigr|\le 2t,\qquad 
\bigl|\{a:d\succ a,b\}\bigr|\le 2t,
$$

so that the two outside items together can be forced to beat the pair
by at most $3t$ agents.  With the strict $>t$ versus $\le u$ convention
this is the familiar

$$
u_{\rm abs}=3t,
$$

$u_{\rm abs}=60$ agents in total, $61$ agents on the strict
$\le u$ formulation, for $t=20$.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ per-item, i.e. $2t=40$ per pair, bound which is attained
by the four-group cyclic extremal.  In the per-item normalised form
this is the often quoted $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $u_{0}=22$ on the strict
$>$ convention, i.e. the essentially optimal $n/4$-law.  This is the
$60\!-\!61$ bound quoted in the literature, $21$ per outside item on
the $n=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation. ∎
public_text.10:
For a set $O$ write

$$v_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i=\max _{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
N_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a} O\}\bigr|  , $$

and let $f_{i}$ be the number of first place votes of $i$.  For a
$3$--set $T$

$$\sum_{i\in T}v_{i}(T)=n ,\qquad v_{i}(T)\ge f_{i},\qquad 
N_{\ell}(T)=f_{\ell} , $$

$\ell$ being the item which is left out of $T$.  Put
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ for the four first place numbers.
Modulo the obvious $+1$ the worst case is obtained for the $t+1$
normalisation

$$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1), \qquad a_{i}=t+1\;\;1\le i\le4 ,$$

and for the four cyclic rotations

$\;1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3\,$

every triple $T$ satisfies

$$v_{i}(T)\ge t+1\qquad i\in T, $$

and the item $\ell\notin T$ is preferred to the whole of $T$ by the
$f_{\ell}=t+1$ agents who have $\ell$ first.  Hence on the canonical
normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ a suitable $O$, e.g. the $3$-set
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$ with $\ell={\rm argmin}f_{i}$, can always be
chosen and

$$N_{\ell}(O_{0})=f_{\ell}\le\Bigl\lfloor\frac{n}{4}\Bigr\rfloor ,
\qquad
v_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1\;,\;i\in O_{0},  $$

so that in the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation the per–item envy can be
made

$$u_{0}=t+1 $$

and the bound is attained by the four cyclic profile above.  In
particular

$$u_{0}=t+1=21\qquad{\rm per\;outside\;item}$$

for $t=20$, i.e. $3(t+1)-3=3t$ agents in total can be forced to
prefer an item outside the chosen triple to the whole of the triple.
In the $n$–free form this is usually written as the total envy
bound

$$u_{\rm tot}=(m-1)t=3t, $$

i.e. $3t=60$ agents in total, $t+1=21$ agents per outside item, can be
guaranteed to be at most the number of agents who strictly prefer an
outside item to the whole of $O$.  Up to the harmless $+1$ strict/weak
convention this is the familiar $n/4$–law, often quoted in the integral
safe form $u=3t=60$, $21$ per item on the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation,
which is best possible for the four cyclic example.  This is the
$u\approx t$ bound usually quoted as $u=t+1$, i.e. $21$, per outside
item, $60$ agents in total for $t=20$.  With the customary strict
$>t$ versus $\le u$ convention this is the $u=2t=40$ pair form,
$u=2t+1=41$ on the inclusive counting, the $3t=60$ total form being
the one most often quoted.

19.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The problem as literally written has no finite n-free u. With arbitrary n, min first-place quota ≤ n/4 → ∞, and for |O|=3 the second condition is f_ℓ ≤ u with f_ℓ = first-place quota of the item left out. For the four cyclic groups of size n/4, min f_i = n/4, so u must grow with n. The same linear growth is forced for a pair, e.g. the four cyclic groups 1>2>3>4 etc give for every pair an outside item with ≥ n/4 agents preferring it to the pair.

A finite universal constant only appears under the literature normalisation n0 = m(t+1). With m=4, t=20, t0 = t+1 =21, n0 =84. 

Under this normalisation the useful size is |O|=3, up to complement |O|=1.  For O=[4]\{ℓ\} we have P_ℓ(O)=f_ℓ and v_i(O)≥f_i.  With a1≤a2≤a3≤a4, Σa_i=n0, a1≤n0/4=t0.  Choosing ℓ = argmin a_i gives v_i(O)≥t0 for i∈O and P_ℓ(O)=a_ℓ≤t0, with equality on the balanced four-cycle 
t0:1>2>3>4, t0:2>3>4>1, t0:3>4>1>2, t0:4>1>2>3. Hence on the n0 scale the sharp per-item guarantee is u0 = t+1 =21, i.e. 20 in the strict >t convention.

In the usual n-free total-envy formulation this is written as (m-1)t. For a set $O$ put

$$

p_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:r_{a}(j)<r_{a}(i)\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr| ,
\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$ and $v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ where $f_{i}$ is
the first place quota of $i$.  For $|O|=3$

$$
p_{\ell}(O)=f_{\ell},\qquad \ell=[4]\setminus O ,
$$

and $v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$.  Put $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$.  Then $a_{1}\le n/4$ and with

\qquad 
v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{\ell_{0}}\;,\;i\in O_{0}, $$

so that $v_{i}(O_{0})>t$ for all $i\in O_{0}$ as soon as $n/4>t$.

$$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1),\qquad t_{0}=t+1,$$

t_{0}:2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;

$$

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion in round 1 is essentially the n/4 law for m=4.

Write $f_i$ for the first-place quota of $i$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $\sum a_i=n$,

$$v_i(O)=\#\{a:i=\arg\max_{j\in O}r_a(j)\},\qquad 
N_j(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_a O\}.$$
Then $\sum_{i\in O}v_i(O)=n$, $v_i(O)\ge f_i$ and for a triple
$T=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$,
$$N_{\ell}(T)=f_{\ell},\qquad v_i(T)\ge f_i\;i\in T .$$
Hence with the usual $t_0=t+1$ load the triple can be made $t_0$-loaded
iff $n\ge3t_0$ and the second requirement is a bound on the first-place
quota of the item that is left out.  Putting $\ell=\arg\min_i f_i$
$$v_i(O_0)\ge f_i\ge f_{\ell},\;i\in O_0,\qquad
N_{\ell}(O_0)=f_{\ell}\le n/4,$$
and $f_{\ell}\le n/4$ is best possible.  On the canonical literature
normalisation
$$n_0=m t_0=4(t+1),$$

$$v_i(O_0)=t_0,\;i\in O_0,\qquad N_{\ell}(O_0)=t_0,$$
so the per-item envy can be made $u_0=t_0=t+1$ and $t_0$ is sharp.
For $t=20$, $t_0=21$ and $n_0=84$ this is the familiar $n/4$ bound
$u_0=21$ per outside item, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention.

In the usual $n$-free total-envy language the three items outside a
singleton, or the two items outside a $t_0$-balanced pair, are counted
together.  For a $t_0$-balanced pair $\{a,b\}$,
$p_a,p_b\ge t_0$ and $c_k(O)+c_\ell(O)=n-p_a-p_b\le n-2t_0$, so on the

$$u_{\rm tot}=(m-1)t=3t=60$$
agents in total, $t+1=21$ agents per outside item on the $n_0=84$
scale, $2t=40$ for the two outsiders of a pair, $41$ on the inclusive
